title: "Exercises — Cleanup, quantification and quality control"
---

Pen and paper, and a calculator. Show the units.

# Part 1 — Clean-up

## E1. Double-sided selection

You have 150 µL of sheared and ligated DNA and want to keep roughly 300 to 600 bp. You use a first bead ratio of 0.55× and a final ratio of 0.75×. How much bead suspension do you add at each step, and what do you keep?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The second ratio is relative to the **original** sample volume, and the supernatant from the first step is what you keep.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
First: 0.55 × 150 = 82.5 µL. Keep the supernatant (232.5 µL), discard the beads: they hold the long fragments. Final bead volume 0.75 × 150 = 112.5 µL, so add 112.5 − 82.5 = **30 µL**. Keep the beads, wash and elute: they hold the window between the two cut-offs.
:::

## E2. Pick the clean-up

Choose bead, column, precipitation or gel, and justify:

a. Remove 25 nt primers from a 300 bp PCR product, 50 µL volume
b. Concentrate 0.5 ng of DNA from 500 µL
c. Isolate exactly 200–250 bp from a broad smear
d. Many plates, automated, with a wish for a size cut-off

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Beads at about 1.0×, or a column; both remove short oligos.
b. Precipitation with a carrier (glycogen), since beads or columns would give a low yield from a large volume.
c. A gel slice: the only exact window.
d. Beads, because the ratio sets the cut-off and the step scales.
:::

## E3. A trap: the PEG in the ligation mix

A kit says "add 0.8× beads to the ligation reaction". The reaction contains PEG. You dilute it with water to 100 µL first, then add 0.8× of 100 µL. What changes?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The kit ratio is calibrated for the original volume, with its PEG. Diluting the mix lowers the PEG that the beads see, and adding a different volume of beads sets a different final PEG. The cut-off moves, usually to longer fragments, and adapter dimers may be kept or lost differently. Follow the kit's volume, or calibrate with a ladder.
:::

# Part 2 — Quantification and pooling

## E4. Convert

a. 1.2 ng/µL, mean length 380 bp: concentration in nM?
b. 25 nM, 500 bp: concentration in ng/µL?
c. 4.0 ng/µL by Qubit, a 300 bp insert with 120 bp of adapter: concentration in nM?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 1.2 × 10^6 / (660 × 380) = 1.2 × 10^6 / 250,800 = **4.8 nM**.
b. 25 × 660 × 500 / 10^6 = **8.3 ng/µL**.
c. L = 420: 4.0 × 10^6 / (660 × 420) = **14.4 nM**.
:::

## E5. Pool three libraries

| Library | ng/µL | mean length (bp) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 6.0 | 500 |
| B | 2.5 | 350 |
| C | 12 | 700 |

You want 10 fmol of each in the pool. a. Give the nM of each. b. Give the volumes. c. Which volumes are impractical, and what do you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
1 nM is 1 fmol/µL.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. A: 6.0 × 10^6 / 330,000 = 18.2 nM. B: 2.5 × 10^6 / 231,000 = 10.8 nM. C: 12 × 10^6 / 462,000 = 26.0 nM.
b. A: 10 / 18.2 = 0.55 µL. B: 10 / 10.8 = 0.92 µL. C: 10 / 26.0 = 0.38 µL.
c. A and C are below what a pipette delivers accurately. Dilute A 1 in 4 (4.55 nM, take 2.2 µL) and C 1 in 5 (5.2 nM, take 1.9 µL).
:::

## E6. The disagreement

A library of 450 bp reads 5.0 ng/µL on Qubit, and 3.1 nM by qPCR. What does Qubit predict in nM, what fraction is qPCR-detectable, and what could explain the gap?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Qubit: 5.0 × 10^6 / 297,000 = 16.8 nM. qPCR is 3.1 / 16.8 = about 18%. The rest is DNA without both adapters (one-sided products, unligated fragments), or an artefact of over-amplification; a trace shows which. Load by qPCR, not Qubit.
:::

# Part 3 — Reading traces

## E7. How much of the sequencing is dimer?

A trace shows a main peak at 420 bp holding 85% of the mass, and a dimer peak at 130 bp holding 15%. What fraction of the molecules is dimer?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Molecules = mass / length.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Main: 0.85 / 420 = 0.00202. Dimer: 0.15 / 130 = 0.00115. Dimer fraction = 0.00115 / (0.00202 + 0.00115) = **36% of molecules**, and clustering favours short molecules even more, so the read share is higher. A 15% mass peak is a bigger problem than it looks.
:::

## E8. A shoulder after PCR

After 14 PCR cycles the trace shows the expected peak at 400 bp and a second hump around 1,500 bp. qPCR gives a molarity five times lower than the Qubit prediction. What has happened, and what do you do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Over-amplification: primers were exhausted, so strands annealed through the common adapter regions and formed partly single-stranded, larger products that run slowly and do not prime in qPCR. Quantify by qPCR (the five-fold lower number is the useful one), reduce cycles next time (use a diagnostic qPCR), or add two cycles of fresh primer to convert the heteroduplexes.
:::

# Part 4 — Tricks

## E9. How many more cycles?

You pre-amplify cDNA for 5 cycles, then run 5 µL (10% of the 50 µL reaction) in a qPCR. The aliquot reaches one third of its maximum signal at cycle 7. How many extra cycles do you give the remaining 45 µL?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
7 cycles. The aliquot is only a smaller volume of the same concentration, so it needs the same number of cycles. Total PCR is 5 + 7 = 12 cycles. Stopping at one third of maximum keeps the library from reaching the plateau.
:::

## E10. PhiX tells you the quantification was wrong

You spiked 5% PhiX into a run (so 95% library by loading). The run returns 12% PhiX reads. By what factor did you over-estimate the library concentration?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Compare the PhiX:library ratio of what you loaded with what you got.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Loaded 5:95 = 0.053. Got 12:88 = 0.136. The library produced 0.053/0.136 = 0.39 of the expected clusters, so its concentration was over-estimated about **2.6-fold**: typical of a Qubit-based loading of a library with unclusterable DNA.
:::

# Self-check

1. Why does a higher bead ratio keep shorter fragments?
2. What does qPCR count that Qubit does not?
3. Why do you pool by moles, not mass?
4. Why is a small adapter-dimer peak more serious than its area suggests?
5. Why must a diagnostic qPCR use an aliquot of the same reaction?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. More PEG in the mixture crowds shorter DNA onto the beads.
2. Only molecules with both adapters, which are the ones that can cluster.
3. Equal mass gives more molecules of short libraries, so they would take too many reads.
4. Dimers are short, so mass underestimates their molecule count, and they cluster efficiently.
5. It reports the real concentration and state of that reaction, so the cycle count transfers.
:::
